recipes.name: Pa amb tomàquet
recipes.description: A ripe tomato. Good bread. Your first words in Catalan.

steps.title: Meet your ingredients
steps.guidance: Put the bread, tomato, olive oil and salt on the counter. A good meal can start with just four ingredients.

steps.title: Toast the bread
steps.guidance: Lightly toast two slices until the edges are crisp. Leave a little softness in the middle.

steps.title: Let the tomato do the work
steps.guidance: Cut the tomato in half. Rub the cut side over the warm bread, letting the pulp sink into the surface.

steps.title: A little oil, a little salt
steps.guidance: Drizzle with olive oil, add a pinch of salt, and serve straight away. Point to each ingredient and name it.

story.title: More than something on toast.
story.text: In Catalonia, bread rubbed with tomato is an everyday culinary ritual. The tomato is rubbed directly into the bread, then finished with olive oil. Something so simple becomes a way to share a table.

nameStory.en: The name is refreshingly literal: pa amb tomàquet just means "bread with tomato." The tomato's own name traveled much further to get here — tomàquet reached Catalan through Spanish, which borrowed it from Classical Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, a reminder that tomatoes only reached Europe after the voyages to the Americas.
nameStory.target: El nom és ben literal: pa amb tomàquet vol dir això mateix. Però la paraula tomàquet ha viatjat molt més per arribar aquí — passa pel castellà, que la va prendre del nàhuatl clàssic, la llengua dels asteques, un record que el tomàquet només va arribar a Europa després dels viatges a Amèrica.

regionalNote.title: Rubbed here, grated everywhere else.
regionalNote.text: In Catalonia — Barcelona and Girona alike — the tomato is cut in half and rubbed straight onto the bread, leaving the skin behind like a natural filter. Travel south to Madrid or Andalusia and cooks grate the tomato instead, often mixed with garlic. Girona even holds its own pa amb tomàquet fair each year, in Santa Coloma de Farners, running since 2001.

recipes.name: Escalivada
recipes.description: Roasted vegetables, slow moments, and a few new phrases.

steps.title: A colorful beginning
steps.guidance: Gather and wash your vegetables. Name their colors before you start.

steps.title: Into the oven
steps.guidance: Heat the oven to 200°C. Put the vegetables on a tray and rub with a little oil.

steps.title: Take your time
steps.guidance: Roast for about 35 minutes, turning halfway, until softened. Use this quiet moment to read the story.

steps.title: Peel and share
steps.guidance: Allow to cool enough to handle. Peel and remove seeds, tear into strips, and dress with oil and salt.

story.title: A classic made from vegetables.
story.text: Barcelona’s traditional recipe repertoire includes escalivada: a salad of roasted peppers, aubergines and other vegetables. Here the vegetables themselves take the leading role.

nameStory.en: Escalivada comes from escalivar, Catalan for "to cook in embers" — a direct memory of when these vegetables were roasted straight in the ashes of a wood fire, not in an oven.
nameStory.target: Escalivada ve d'escalivar, que en català vol dir "coure a les brases" — un record directe de quan aquestes verdures es rostien directament a les cendres del foc de llenya, no al forn.

regionalNote.title: One dish, many regional cousins.
regionalNote.text: Escalivada belongs to a whole family of roasted-vegetable dishes across the old Crown of Aragón. Cross into Aragón and the same idea becomes firigolla, with roasted tomato added; head further south and it turns into ensalada asada, with tomato and garlic too. Catalonia keeps its version simple: peppers, aubergine and onion, letting the smoke do the talking.

recipes.name: Panellets
recipes.description: Little almond sweets with a whole season inside them.

steps.title: Meet the autumn table
steps.guidance: Measure the almonds and sugar. Set aside the pine nuts and separate the egg.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.guidance: Mix the almonds, sugar and lemon zest. Add egg white a little at a time to make a workable dough.

steps.title: A moment to rest
steps.guidance: Rest the dough for 20 minutes. Read the Castanyada story while you wait.

steps.title: Roll, then coat
steps.guidance: Shape small balls. Press pine nuts onto the outside and brush lightly with beaten yolk.

steps.title: Into the oven
steps.guidance: Bake on a lined tray at 200°C for about 10 minutes. Let the sweets cool before moving them.

steps.title: Share the story
steps.guidance: Serve your panellets and describe the process in your own words. What makes a food feel festive?

story.title: A little taste of the Castanyada.
story.text: Panellets are eaten during the Castanyada, the chestnut celebration that forms part of All Saints festivities. Seasonal sweets turn a bakery visit into a small encounter with Catalan tradition.

nameStory.en: Panellets simply means "little breads" in Catalan — a modest name for a sweet with deep roots. The ground-almond base shows the influence of Arabic pastry-making, and by the 18th century panellets were already being used as blessed food in religious celebrations.
nameStory.target: Panellets vol dir senzillament "panets petits" en català — un nom modest per a un dolç amb arrels profundes. La base d'ametlla mòlta mostra la influència de la pastisseria àrab, i ja al segle XVIII els panellets es feien servir com a aliment beneït en celebracions religioses.

source.name: Catalan News · The odyssey of panellets

regionalNote.title: Why pine nuts, here.
regionalNote.text: Panellets come in many shapes — pyramidal coconut ones, cylindrical almond ones — but around Barcelona, pine nut panellets are the clear local favourite, accounting for roughly half of what's eaten each autumn. That's the version this lesson teaches.

say.ca: Tens ametlla, sucre i un ou?
say.en: Do you have almonds, sugar and an egg?
How do you say “egg” in Catalan?

say.ca: Barreja l'ametlla i el sucre al bol.
say.en: Mix the almond and the sugar in the bowl.
Done? (Send a photo if you like.)

say.ca: Afegeix l'ou a poc a poc.
say.en: Add the egg little by little.
The dough rests for twenty minutes.
How many minutes? Say it in Catalan.

conversation.culture: While it rests: panellets are eaten during the Castanyada, the chestnut celebration that is part of the All Saints festivities. (Source: Barcelona Tourism.)

say.en: Make little balls and press pine nuts on.

say.ca: Al forn! Dos-cents graus, deu minuts.
say.en: Into the oven! 200 degrees, ten minutes.

say.ca: Bona Castanyada! Ho has fet molt bé.
say.en: Happy Castanyada! You did very well.

criteria: Pieces are small and roughly the same size
Rounded balls or ovals, not flattened into discs

criteria: Pine nuts cover most of the outside of each piece

Colour is even across the tray
